idiom_name: one destination per message type + per-channel codec (or the language's typed channel primitive)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every message type its own channel - queue, topic, subscription or in-process channel - and let the channel's identity be the type binding, so producers publish by type and consumers subscribe per type and never inspect a type discriminator. Materialize the type-to-channel mapping in one governed place (naming convention, constant table, schema-registry subject, broker topology) and give every channel its own decoder/validator and delivery policy: retention, ordering, retry, dead-letter destination and access control. Where the language or runtime can enforce the binding statically - a generic channel, a typed mailbox, a typed stream - use that instead of documentation; where it cannot (untyped queue, REST endpoint), validate at the boundary and reject mismatched payloads to an invalid-message channel. In distributed deployments, pair with a schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry for Kafka, Redpanda Schema Registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry) so that schema IDs are embedded in messages and consumers can fetch the correct schema by ID, enabling independent schema evolution per channel.
code_sketch:
types:   Order -> "orders" | Invoice -> "invoices" | Reading -> "readings"

publish(value):  ch = channel_for(type_of(value)); ch.send(encode(value))
consume(ch):     for msg in ch: handle(decode_as(type_of(ch), msg))   # type from channel identity
on decode error: invalid_message_channel.send(ch, msg, reason)
pitfalls: Sending a second type on an existing channel 'just this once': the receiver's decoder, validation, monitoring and ACL are now wrong for half the traffic.
Creating channels dynamically per instance or per schema version instead of per type, which makes the topology unbounded and unmanageable.
No per-channel error path, so a decoding failure either stalls the type's consumer or drops messages silently.
Hard-coding channel names as string literals across repositories: refactoring silently diverges and creates orphan channels; derive names from a single constants map or enum.
In distributed brokers, using a shared consumer group for all types so a slow consumer of one type stalls producers of unrelated types.
Publishing messages without a schema ID or content-type header, so consumers cannot decode when schema evolves.
Neglecting to set per-channel dead-letter or retry topology, so poison messages sit in the main queue indefinitely.

Wrong move: splitting one aggregate's or entity's events into one topic per type -> consumers reading several topics see 'address changed' before 'customer created' and timestamps cannot recover the order -> instead keep all events of one entity in the same channel partitioned by entity id, and reserve per-type channels for unrelated flows.

Wrong move: one channel per type no matter how rare the traffic -> thousands of low-throughput topics become thousands of partitions, and per-broker latency, memory and failure-recovery times degrade (topic explosion) -> instead merge fine-grained low-rate types into coarser channels and keep dedicated channels for high-throughput or access-control-sensitive types.

Wrong move: treating per-type channel naming alone as the type guarantee -> a producer with a stale or wrong schema still publishes an incompatible payload to the 'right' channel and the consumer's decoder breaks anyway -> instead pair the channel binding with registry-enforced schema subjects (e.g. Kafka's default TopicNameStrategy) or per-channel schema validation.
sources: Hohpe, G. & Woolf, B., Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) - Datatype Channel.
